extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, literary critics, and theorists of comedy/humour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical criteria for creating and analysing comic characters/types in comedy (especially dramatic/comedic poetry), focusing on what makes a character laughable, how comedy differs from tragedy, and methods for producing generalisable comic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy depicts general types (stock characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every comic character is a type. Comedy depicts characters, that is, general types; it is the only one of all the arts that aims at the general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic works should present characters that read as representatives of a class rather than unique individuals; titles and character-names often slide into common nouns (e.g., Le Misanthrope, L'Avare) because the play presents a type rather than a unique psyche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be capable of self-repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic poet's object is to offer us types, that is, characters capable of self-repetition; it even creates new types, if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fix a comic type, dramatists often show several different copies or satellites of the same model so that the peculiarity appears as a category into which many individuals can step — similar to how a naturalist defines a species by enumerating varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation directed outwards (others, not self)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy springs from an outward observation: however interested a dramatist may be in comic features, he will hardly try to discover his own; it is on others that such observation must be practised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic writing relies on noticing external traits and behaviours in other people rather than introspective access to one's own hidden ridiculousness; this yields general, reproducible effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic observation must be superficial/skin-deep
rubrics_metrics.description: Settling on the surface, [comic observation] will not be more than skin-deep, dealing with persons at the point at which they come into contact and become capable of resembling one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penetrate too far into personality or deep causes; localise the cause of the laughable in an intermediate region of the soul so the effect remains laughable and immediately correctible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise cause in partially externalised attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: To be laughable, a mental attribute must resemble absentmindedness, something that lives upon him without forming part of his organism, after the fashion of a parasite; it is observable from without and capable of being corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic traits should appear detachable and correctible — not essential, deep-seated pathologies — so that laughter can serve its corrective social function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of comedy: corrective social function
rubrics_metrics.description: By organising laughter, comedy accepts social life as a natural environment...it has a scarcely confessed or scarcely conscious intention to correct and instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic effects to expose and correct social inconveniences (e.g., vanity) through laughter; comedy's verdict should incline toward social instruction rather than art-for-art's-sake idealisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as the principal laughable failing
rubrics_metrics.description: This mixture [most widespread through mankind] is vanity...the specific remedy for vanity is laughter, and the one failing that is essentially laughable is vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for manifestations of vanity (self-admiration, exaggerated self-regard) as fertile material for comedy; many coarse comic effects are ultimately traced to perceived vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic types must be paradoxically deep-rooted yet superficial
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be deep-rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy; invisible to its actual owner, but visible to everybody else; immediately repressible, but sure of reappearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct comic characters whose propensities are stable enough to yield recurring humour but sufficiently surface-level to be exposed and (in social terms) corrected; include traits that the character does not perceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be considerate to themselves but troublesome to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely considerate to its own self, so that it may be displayed without scruple, but troublesome to others, so that they may repress it without pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic behaviour often arises from self-centered rationalisations that make the character blind to the harm or absurdity perceived by others — exploit that asymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits should be readily repressible yet recurrent
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately repressible, so that our laughter may not have been wasted, but sure of reappearing under fresh aspects, so that laughter may always find something to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic actions that can be checked in scene but plausibly recur in different forms, enabling repeated laughter without exhausting the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters must be inseparable from social life
rubrics_metrics.description: Inseparable from social life, although insufferable to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Root comic traits in social contexts (vanity, self-display, ritualised behaviour) so they resonate broadly; make characters socially embedded so their follies affect others and permit social correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy uses abstraction and generalisation (inductive method)
rubrics_metrics.description: This [comic] observation instinctively proceeds to what is general...in short by a process of abstraction and generalisation similar to that which the physicist brings to bear upon facts with the object of grouping them under laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create types, compare analogous cases, extract essences, and present the generalized trait rather than idiosyncratic detail; treat comic creation analytically like empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy contrasts with tragedy (generality vs individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Altogether different is the object of comedy...the essential difference between tragedy and comedy, the former being concerned with individuals and the latter with classes, is revealed in yet another way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for comic effect, avoid the tragic focus on unique inner life and complex individuality; instead emphasise reproducible traits and external behaviour that indicate a class/type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and labels promote generality
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not see the actual things themselves; in most cases we confine ourselves to reading the labels affixed to them...words (with the exception of proper nouns) all denote genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stereotyped speech, stock phrases and labels to cue types quickly; the linguistic tendency to name genera helps make characters immediately legible as types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effects can derive from subtle elements or their degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any simple image, laughable in itself, is capable of worming its way into other images of a more complex nature and instilling into them something of its comic essence; the inverse process...many coarse comic effects are the direct result of a drop from some very subtle comic element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ both subtle psychological insights and their coarse echoes — sometimes amplifying or mislocating a subtle trait (e.g., projecting vanity) produces stronger, cruder laughs; be aware of how a high comic element can degrade into a low one.

rubrics_metrics.name: All peculiarities (even virtues) can be comic if they form a category
rubrics_metrics.description: We have shown that all failings may become laughable, and even, occasionally, many a good quality...The essential condition...is that the peculiarity observed should straightway appear as a kind of category into which a number of individuals can step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't limit comic material to vices: identify patterns (including virtues taken to an extreme) that can be generalized into types; the key is reproducibility across individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create types by grouping similar secondary characters around a central model
rubrics_metrics.description: A remarkable instinct impels the comic poet, once he has elaborated his central character, to cause other characters, displaying the same general traits, to revolve as satellites round him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structuring a play or sketch, populate the world with supporting characters who mirror or amplify the central type to make the class visible and to produce multiplied comic situations.
